qT
142 CHAPTER 5
sively. (The previously mentioned patient had a character disorder, and all the
patients referred to here were seen in private practice while they were carrying on
gainful activities and were certainly not frankly psychotic.) |
When the mechanism of avoidance is used, the T.A.T. material may be long
and apparently very rich, yet it will defy analysis. This is, of course, the experience |
with any form of output of manics or hypomanics. Fortunately at least one story
usually turns out to contain the real core, while the others have such an over-
growth of defense that it requires very special pains and an awareness of the t
centrifugal nature of the material to be able to use it. With manics and other i
predominantly oral character disorders, the most useful story usually turns out to
be the one told to picture 11. The theme of devouring, which this Boecklin f
picture suggests, contains precisely the stimulus this group responds to. \
The defenses revealed by the T.A.T. are identical with those appearing in
free associations and in dreams. Those patients who give the most frustrating
T.A.T. stories may spend hours on seemingly irrelevant material and recount :
long, involved dreams more suitable for Hollywood scenarios than for analysis.
Itis a fact, then, that, by and large, T.A.T. records do not always permit one '
to identify the presenting clinical symptoms. In the records of two pronouncedly i I
agoraphobic women there is nothing to indicate manifest agoraphobia; in the s
records of three severely anorexic women there is nothing that shows the present- : 7
ing problem of anorexia. : ,
This is purely a matter of methodological interest, part of the problem of :
the relationship of the overt to the latent. I see no reason why one should need the i I
T.A.T. to identify a clinical syndrome; ask the patient—she will be glad to tell you : is
that she is agoraphobic or anorexic. I
However, the T.A.T. was very useful in all these cases in reflecting the i : :
underlying dynamics. It showed the ambivalence, the exhibitionism, and the fear ) :
of aggression in the agoraphobes, as well as the figures the aggression was j :
directed against. A posteriori, one could identify all the component parts that i :
belonged to the picture. An exception may be the quantitative aspects; as in :
dreams and fantasies, it is difficult to appraise the strength of the variables }
involved, and it would be difficult to predict whether they are strong enough to
turn up as manifest syndrome formation. With a study of defenses, however, this { 7
is not impossible. There have been a number of records, particularly of the ‘ i
C.A.T., where I could successfully predict anorexia as a clinical syndrome, al- \
though at times only a detailed consideration of the defenses permitted me to i I
differentiate between overeating and anorexia. t
These observations of mine are entirely in agreement with the excellent ; 8
theoretical formulations which Sargent presents in her pyramid of diagnostic a
inference (Figures 5—1 and 5-2). She states that after a consideration of the raw
data of the tests comes a level of generalization; then a second inferential level of : ¥
theoretical interpretation; and only then a third (abstract) inference as to the b
classificatory diagnosis. She demonstrates the overlapping of the two levels of d
inference for two (or more) diagnostic labels. 4 t
I realized long ago how well the identifying features of psychodynamics and fi
character structure can be revealed in the T.A.T. when I gave it to patients in ¢
analysis and found a high level of agreement; often the analysts found that the i u

The Problem of Overt and Latent Needs in the T.A.T.* \
The interpreter of T.A.T. stories is frequently presented with the necessity of ;
deciding whether or not a need expressed pertains strictly to the fantasy level or i
might be expressed in reality, for example, the need for aggression or for |
achievement. The psychologist should have available a maximum of clinical and :
biographical data about the patient. It must be kept in mind that the clinical \
situation is not one concerned with testing the validity of the instrument. Prob-
lems of the validity of the T.A.T. are dealt with in experiments and must be | :
decided there. If one has sufficient information on the patient, then the T.A.T. :
stories must be seen as complementary to the behavioral data obtained. For i
example, if the subject is unduly shy and retiring and the stories are full of i
aggression and guilt feelings, the dynamic implications are obvious. :
On the other hand, there are certain indications from intratest situations i
which permit us to make assumptions about the manifest or latent needs. ex- 1
pressed in the T.A.T. For instance, in stories of achievement it is extremely
important to notice whether they follow the deus ex machina mechanism or are |
actually accomplished piece by piece, suggesting much more that they cor- :
respond to a behavioral need for achievement.
It was R. N. Sanford who pointed out some important rules concerning the :
relationship between fantasy needs and behavioral needs. He suggested that j
there are certain needs that are usually high in fantasy and low in behavior, :
namely, those needs which are usually prohibited and inhibited by cultural pres- :
sure from overt manifestation. These are mainly the needs of acquisition, aggres- i
sion, autonomy, and sexual activity, the wish to be taken care of, and the need for i
harm avoidance, the last two suffering more cultural repression in men. On the : :
other hand, some needs may find little manifest expression in fantasy but may i
find much expression in manifest behavior because of reality demands, such as
the need for order, for avoiding social blame, for learning. Again, there is a class
of needs which may be high both in fantasy and in behavior, indicating that, while :
these needs are permitted and encouraged socially, they may yet be sufficiently :
frustrated to need particular gratification on the fantasy level. To these belong
especially the needs for achievement, for friendship, and for dominance. i

Insight. Insight development is the next step in the therapeutic process. The
term insight is abused almost as much as the term psychotherapy itself. Fre-
quently the term insight is used to mean simply that the patient is aware of being
mentally ill. This is most often used in the discussion of psychotics, usually
implying no more than just that. In the context of dynamic psychotherapy,
| insight must have this specific meaning—the patient's ability to see the relationship
between a given symptom and the previously unconscious apperceptive distortions underly-
ing his symptoms. More strictly speaking, we define insight as the patient’s apper-
| ception (i.e., meaningful perception) of the common denominators of his behav-
i ior as pointed out by the therapist. The problem is seen in a new light and
| : handled differently from then on.
| This process may be analyzed into two parts:

I class or, in Gestalt language, he learns by insight and experiences closure. The
r : pieces of isolated happenings become a memory whole, and a repatterning and
4 i relearning takes place.
z ! 2. Emotional insight: The patient reproduces the affect pertaining to the
5 | intellectual insight—relief, anxiety, guilt, happiness, and the like. a
e If the intellectual insight alone is produced, limited or no therapeutic result
e i may be achieved because emotional repatterning is an essential of the therapeutic
i | process, be it conceived of as a regular libidinal-metapsychologic process or as a

1€ : be part of the Gestalt of a therapeutic experience.

D. Diagnostic Aspects in Relation to Therapy* | Hit
|
Psychological testes have much the same relationship to psychotherapy as clinical | asp
pathological tests and x-rays have to general medicine. Like the medical man, the | aa
psychotherapist should have a basic knowledge of testing procedures in order to
be able to request the appropriate one, and should understand the basic meaning 1
well enough to be able to integrate the test results with the additional data. As in \ |
general medicine, the therapist should not blindly rely upon the test results, nor | 2
should he expect from them an exact diagnostic answer to every problem. Itis the i 3
clinician’s job to make a careful clinical evaluation and to integrate all the factors. } 4
No test can be a substitute for clinical knowledge and acumen. It is inappropriate { 5
for the psychotherapist to expect an answer to all his problems from the psycholo- | q
gist, and for the psychologist to offer definitive statements without knowing the i
clinical situation. When I play the role of psychologist, I prefer to offer my data as i
“consistent with” such and such a disorder (i.e., “This patient's record is consistent f Bae
with a sadomasochistic character disorder”). | ie :
Psychological tests may be helpful in diagnosis, if diagnosis does not imply f a,
simply attaching labels to a patient, but rather implies gauging liabilities and | fe
assets; if diagnosis involves therapeutic planning and prognostication, the great ‘ | Me
significance of the tests is obvious. AG h
If I restrict myself to the projective personality tests, then it seems to me that | 5 i
they can be divided into two kinds: those concerned essentially with testing formal 7 1 a
quantitative aspects (which I increasingly believe indicate primarily degrees of aS ae
ego strength) and those which reveal content (dynamics). 4 h
Of the first category, the Rorschach is the main representative; of the tia
second, the T.A.T. It should be kept in mind that this division is somewhat : my
arbitrary, in that the Rorschach may elicit some indications of interpersonal rs a
relations and the T.A.T. may offer some ego strength indicators. abe aes

| | From the standpoint of therapy, the quantitative indicators may permit one
to gauge the amount of strain and stress to which a patient may be safely exposed
by interpretations and transference tensions; the content tests supply the sub-
stance of the pesonality itself, like dreams and fantasies made to order.
The quantitative indicators are predicated upon the probing of subsemantic
levels, by studying neuromuscular expressions (as in figure drawing) or percep-
; tual patterns (as in the Rorschach). Thus they may reveal motivations that are
: unconscious in the sense of never having had any verbal representations. A
brace breakthrough of aggressive impulses due to a brain defect may often be covered
> up verbally while it will manifest itself myoneurally (e.g., in a drawing). The
: content tests reveal particularly well matters that are unconscious in the psycho-
analytic sense.
| More detailed principles of classification of what is usually subsumed under
| projective tests might be helpful for the clinical selection of proper tests for
\ therapeutic purposes. These suggestions will indicate only the primary useful
| aspects of certain tests and will not ignore the fact that each test contributes on
: ' several levels.
: I believe that one may group available techniques under five headings:
|
g | 1. Methods based on the study of content: The T.A.T., C.A.T., and S.A.T
f ‘ 2. Study of expressive, perceptual, structural aspects: Mira, Mosaic, Rorschach,
nl | and graphology
\ 3. Gestalt functions: Bender-Gestalt, Mosaic, Rorschach
i | 4. Body-image or self-image: Figure Drawing, T.A.T., Rorschach
ie 5. Methods of preference: Szondi
. | It is apparent that all five organismic aspects enter into every one of the
= projective methods, although in varying degrees. One might keep these catego-
a | ries in mind for the selection of techniques for each individual problem of
| i diagnosis and therapy—either for the purpose of arranging a rounded battery or
y i for selecting the one test for a specific clinical need. One might use these five
a | variables for a systematic inquiry into the test results of any one technique.
a | A more general classification scheme, relevant to the choice of tests for
therapeutic purposes, derives from the “levels hypothesis,” which has generally
ae , been interpreted as meaning that the less the structure of the test, the deeper the
7 i level of personality being tapped. For example, Stone and Dellis (1960) found
of | that the Wechsler-Bellevue, Forer Sentence Completion Test, T.A.T., Rors-
\ chach, and Draw-A-Person Test reached successively lower, or more primitive,
7 | impulse control systems in their subjects. In a similar vein, Theiner (1962) has
it \ noted greater frequency of acceptable needs expressed in response to a relatively
i ' structured test (Rotter Incomplete Sentence Test), and greater frequency of
| unacceptable needs on the T.A.T. (less structured).
Again, it is feasible that this “levels” principle can be used either toward the
: selection of a specific test in order to obtain specific kinds of information or
ea ; toward the selection of several tests to secure a more global picture of the
i individual.

E. Some Contraindications to the Use of Psychological Tests

|
A brief statement is in order concerning contraindications for psychological tests, for i R
whatever purpose they may be used. Meyer (1951) has published a paper on this |
topic. He is particularly concerned with the effect of the prospect of testing upon |
the patient (in terms of keeping or breaking appointments) and with how testing | R
affects the continuation of therapy. By examining extensive clinical records, he |
finds that testing does not generally have an adverse effect. However, he suggests i T
seven contraindications to testing in order to avoid disturbing consequences: | ,

1. Acute psychosis, incipient psychosis, or acute anxiety states | O

2. Extreme difficulty in establishing relationships (where adjustment to an additional
person would be an undue burden) i

3. Any likelihood that the patient will interpret referral for testing as disinterest on the : :
part of the therapist i

4. Likelihood that referral will be interpreted as evidence of incompetence of the :
therapist |

5. A specific fear of “test” situations in life and a tendency to run away from them i A. :

6. The possibility that testing material might stimulate more material than seems |
desirable at the time (incipient psychosis?)

7. Any indication that the therapeutic situation at the time of referral seems to make th
testing inadvisable, whereas it might be advisable at a later, more suitable date. | spor
These points seems to comprise the most careful consideration published ae

thus far on the entire subject of the testing situation from the point of view of the i a
patient-therapist relationship. H aoe
I have frequently used the test myself with patients in acute anxiety states cael
and severe depressions without any untoward effects. In all cases judgment must 1 nee
be used, and if extra precautions are taken to create a nontraumatic atmosphere, } ee
tests may still be very useful; in fact, in many acute conditions, when the patient is | likel
otherwise unable to profit by communications, the tests may be easier for him to / fen
deal with and may focus on the very core of the problems. ' at fle

| A. Stimulus Value of the T.A.T.
ns
- | It has long been recognized that, in order to properly interpret thematic re-
| : sponses, it is of primary importance to take into account the influence of the
\ stimulus itself in determining the response. Goldfried and Zax (1965) have
ed \ investigated this area and concluded that in evaluating T.A.T. themes it is neces-
he : sary to make interpretations only with regard to the stimulus value of the specific
} card. They obtained ratings of all the T.A.T. cards on 10 bipolar adjectival scales,
~ such as happy-sad. The ratings indicated that the cards vary a good deal as to their
a | ambiguity, that is, the number of scales that consistently describe the picture. It
rey { was also observed that the stimulus properties of some cards are such that it is
au | likely they will “pull” negatively toned stories. Specifically, it was found that for
to : certain cards (e.g., 2, 5) the stimulus pull is weak enough to assume that the story
i reflects the inner state of the subject; on the other hand, for pictures such as 4 and
| 13MF, the stimulus properties of the card are likely to be more responsible for the
| resultant story than are the subject’s inner needs.
t A few other studies have been reported that investigated the effect of
\ stimulus properties on the expression of specific needs or personality variables.
| Lubin (1960) tested the effects of T.A.T. cards whose stimulus properties elicit
: the expression of either sex or aggression. The significant effect of the stimulus
' properties of cards of sexual and aggressive expression was interpreted as indi-
\ cating that certain dimensions (Kagan, 1959) of the T.A.T. response are deter-
j mined by stimulus configurations. Murstein (1962) studied the projection of
| hostility on the T.A.T. as a function of stimulus, background, and personality
\ variables. The stimulus properties of the cards used accounted for more than half
| of the total variance. Murstein concluded that the results provide evidence that
i the stimulus is definitely the most important determinant of the content of a
\ T.A.T. response.
\ Another possible way in which the stimulus properties may influence re-
i sponses has been investigated in studies that have dealt with the effects of simi-
) larity between the subject and certain characteristics of the T.A.T. figures.

B. Sample Variables a
d
Illustrative examples of the possible influences of certain sample variables upon P
thematic responses are contained in the following studies. Sex differences in | b
fantasy patterns have been found by May (1966), who deduced from clincally i t
oriented studies the types of sequences to be expected in men’s and in women’s i it
fantasies. In women’s fantasy, it was hypothesized that there would be reflected { tl

the sequence in feminine masochism: suffering followed by joy, failure followed i

by success. Fantasies of men were expected to reflect the pattern of ascension i n

; Somerset Maugham’s stories fall somewhere between the two extremes of

i direct biography and self-exclusion. Manifestly, source material comes from all

q over the world, Europe, Russia, the Far East. However, Maugham’s personality
shines through all of them.

Thirty of Maugham’s (1953) stories were selected randomly from two vol-
umes, picked by the present author's then 6-year-old daughter and by their
numerical characteristicp—1, 2, 11, 12, 21, 22. I think that even the very statisti-
cally minded, if they knew Maugham, would not object to this simple procedure
of selection. It will become quite clear that the themes and characteristics that
become manifest in the selected stories have a great similarity to most of the rest
of Maugham’s writings, including his major work, Of Human Bondage, which is
considered to be in large part autobiographical. :

D. Discussion -
The external features and the geographical settings of Maugham’s stories vary a ‘ T
great deal. If one compares him, for instance, with Tennessee Williams, it is !
obvious that he is not constricted with regard to milieu. Williams almost always | V
chooses the setting of the American South. Yet I believe that Maugham shares i
with Williams the constrictions of essential subject matter. Whether the adven- | A
tures are in Malaya or India, Chicago or Petrograd, the theme and its treatment H
stay fairly constant. Control of the emotions, the difficulties people get themselves |
into if they do not control them, and especially the dangers to men in their :
feelings for women are the leitmotifs that govern his work. A certain aloof 1
compassion goes hand in hand with urbanity. Stylistically one always notes a form |
of prompt dispatch in the tightly organized plots. There is constriction here, a }
measure of stereotype, within the creative personality. | A.
Freud, in his paper on the poet, mentioned perceptual selectivity with |
regard to the causal relationship between a writer’s productions and his personal- \ Psy
ity. In the case of Maugham, it seems that his stories are the result of such a \ Pro
selective viewing of life. They are the product of the forms of adaptation and | eXE
defenses with which he tried to deal with his own life and his own emotional i
problems. We have some clues as to what these emotional problems might be. \ “su
There are some suggestive relations among his feelings for women, the loss of his | bat
mother at an early age, his aggression and his stammer, his personal shyness, his | ‘ san
marital difficulties, and his restless wanderings. However, these conjectures with t bys
regard to causal interrelations to the early life history are not of central concern to |
us and could not progress beyond the usual state of loose guesses on the basis of | elal
limited material. We are on safer ground if we limit ourselves to inferences : um
covering the relationship between literary production and the personality of the {-
author. \ tha’
One can speculate further: In what way can the kind of story analysis we [> ite
have done here contribute to the understanding and critical analysis of literature? | the |
The systematic frame of reference for analysis of literary products may be gener- 1 om
ally useful for any author’s work. The range and depth of a literary piece are ae Anc
often at the center of critical appraisal, and a T.A.T. type of analysis may well give . sug
a more reliable account than the customary free-style appraisal. Perhaps one of | a ete
the reasons for widely differing critiques may be, at least in part, the lack of any f oft
base line of comparison. |
The type of psychological analysis presented here may well throw some io ae
interesting light on the relationship between an author's personality and his work. ae ae
I do not know that such enlightenment would add anything to the values of i bui
literature, but it might add some interesting facets to the story of man and his 1o fan
behavior. a chil

social interactions among these story characters. The main characters can be A. I
viewed as the more conscious self, while the other, secondary characters can be | C

qualities and the level of reality-testing can be investigated in order to determine | pers
the pathological level of these object relations in the T.A.T. protocol. | bore

be A. Brief Overview of the Diagnostic Concept
eS | of Borderline and Narcissistic Disorders
e i
ite | i Two very popular psychiatric diagnoses of the past decade are the narcissistic
ine | personality disorder intensively studied by Heinz Kohut (1971, 1977), and the
| borderline personality disorder intensively studied by Otto Kernberg (1975,
ler | 1980). Other individuals made substantial contributions prior to, concurrent
ith { with, and subsequent to the contributions of Kohut and Kernberg. Their own
wo | prolific writings and those of a substantial number of disciples have aroused a
in | great deal of interest (Bellak, 1982, 1983).
| The significant factor in both diagnoses is the identification of a psychiatric
i disorder that is characteristically pre-oedipal, rather than an oedipal level neu-
\ rotic disorder (obsessive-compulsive, hysterical, or phobic neurosis), but is possi-
| bly, except for brief episodes, not psychotic. Earlier, the term borderline referred
} to an individual at the border between psychotic and neurotic disorders. This
\ could be a stable disposition or a labile one. It was Kernberg’s contribution to
j insist that borderline designated a specific diagnostic entity with distinct criteria in
: terms of object relations and defenses and called for specific therapeutic man-
\ agement.
( Narcissistic pathology was also earlier thought of as referring to a psychotic
| patient’s withdrawal into a fantasy world of his or her own without a realistic
i relationship to the needs, perceptions, and existence of other people. However,
i narcissistic features could also be seen in a neurotic individual, as in someone who
| wants a circle of noncritical admirers or someone who marries a famous person.
| The dictionary defines narcissism as love of the self at the expense of love for
\ others (as putting one’s own needs above those of everyone else and a lack of
\ empathy for and sensitivity to other people’s feelings). This latter definition is the
{ key factor in narcissistic personality disorder. In Kohut's theory, the development

Neither Kohut’s nor Kernberg’s concepts are generally accepted by psycho-
analysts. The Kris study group (Abend, Porter, & Willick, 1983) on borderline i
conditions at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute did not find a circumscribed 6.
condition as defined by Kernberg and had doubts about the appropriateness and
usefulness of his delineation. Psychoanalysis had usually accepted the coexistence
of pre-oedipal and oedipal aspects in various admixtures and to varying degrees : 7.
in virtually all neuroses and other conditions. Kohut’s complex and rather idio- ie
syncratic formulations have found similar critique. Nevertheless, the borderline |
concept as well as that of the narcissistic personality, without rigid definitions, oe 8.
have merit as heuristic hypotheses. l 9.
Diagnosis of psychotic process in psychological tests in general is well oe
covered by Weiner (1966). Psychotic process on the T.A.T. is seen in the presence qe
of direct sexual and aggressive themes, themes of persecution, characters magi- Be 10.
cally transforming from one thing to another, themes of omnipotence, magical te
power, figures being part one thing and part another, juxtaposition of extremes aE
(angels and devils, acts of murder and loving tenderness), ideas of reference 2 IL
(thinking one card is connected to another card previously given), disorientation ie
and confusion as to person, place, and time, lack of clear body boundaries, and S 12,
gross deviation from the stimulus. The more one sees these indicators on psycho- L 13.
logical tests, the greater the possibility that the individual is either actively psy- i
chotic, has a latent psychosis, or has psychotic features. The frequency of indica- ee
tors helps decide the severity of the condition. ee
Another useful method was pioneered by Anna Freud (1965). Hers was a Le dev
developmental approach to diagnosis, called the “Developmental Profile.” The Le
idea is to identify in the clinical material (social history, set of referring symptoms, fee eng
therapy sessions, and psychological tests) the predominant level of development ie thre
in the area of psychosexual phases (oral, anal, oedipal, latency, adolescence, etc.), ie scre
aggression, interpersonal object relations, defense mechanisms, and other areas. i sim
A clinician who sees severely disturbed individuals for testing can begin with the ie wot
item approach of looking for a large number of indicators of psychotic process ' cop
and then consider a developmental diagnosis. Here the key question is whether de a tr
the person tested is predominantly pre-oedipal (stuck on a level typical of a child te chil
from birth to age 3 years) or oedipal neurotic (3 years and above). 7 figu

Primitive splitting rather than ambivalence is the key feature for borderline
pathology according to Kernberg (1976). He defines primitive splitting as the
keeping apart of extreme affects of love and hate, extreme impulses of aggression
i and libido, and extreme images of the self and of other people (called self and
: object representations) that are characterized as “all good loving” and “all bad
tic hating.” One sees T.A.T. characters that are either angels or devils, good guys or
totally evil ones, without evidence of story figures who are somewhat good and
somewhat bad, who have more than one side to their personalities. Volkan (1976)
speaks of such fantasies of borderline patients as being all in black and white,
off rather than in technicolor. Ambivalence is seen in the T.A.T. by such statements
as “either this. . . or that.” Splitting in narrative style would be something more

on, A continuing debate in the literature is over what is the key issue in border-
are line pathology. Some feel it is separation anxiety and the lack of appropriate

reaction to anxiety, rather than having developed a signal function to anxiety.
ind Some feel it is due to a fragmented, split, or “unintegrated” ego that needs to
da ; develop further towards integration (Winnicott, 1965). Some feel it may be
at fundamentally influenced by organic factors, such as neuropsychological dys-
ind ‘ function in the area of perceptual, perceptual-motor, and motoric integration so
Phe ] that the individual has basic deficits in synthesizing functions and is thus prone to
cks \ fragmentation and unorganized panic under stress. Others emphasize the pre-
the dominant use of primitive splitting and related defenses, such as denial, idealiza-
nes tion, devaluation, and projective identification, rather than repression and its
and : related defenses of reaction formation, rationalization, intellectualization, and
vith : sublimation.

Comment
The more common story to this card is of a child dog doing something wrong, :
such as drinking from the toilet bowl, so the parent dog gives it a spanking. To
this scene, he instead leaves out the spanking, which may be an attempt to deny
the punitive side of his mother that he seems to have expressed in other stories,
particularly the previous one. He may wish to distance himself from this, so he
changes it to the mother looking like she wanted to cut his toe nails, “but it wasn’t
that, she just had to go to the bathroom, too.” It may look like the mother is
punishing (or to him castrating), but she just wants to go to the bathroom as the
child wants to keep the mother from going to the bathroom. Perhaps he sees
himself and his mother or parents as in competition with each other over basic
needs.

Summary : |
The overall picture is of a child with narcissistic pathology, who seems to feel very |
inadequate, unnurtured, unprotected, and threatened by a hostile and cold |
world. In such a world, people do not seem to be loving to each other and he does
not appear to receive any genuine help and care from anyone. Other people
threaten, boast, intimidate, and seem to give him unrealistic things to do that he |
feels totally inadequate attempting, such as Babe Ruth asking the baby chicks to \
pinch run for him in the World Series. In this type of world, everyone—the adult
and the child figures—all seem to end up failing, falling in the mud, or melting
away like cold ice cream. i

psychological characteristics are also beginning to be assessed on the projective

This chapter is a beginning sketch toward considering how neuropsycho-
logical characteristics may be expressed on the T.A.T., C.A.T., and S.A.T. After
discussing Lezak’s (1983) list of neuropsychological indicators on the T.A.T. and
adding items from our own clinical experience, we will present two stories of a
child and adult case with Attention Deficit Disorder (A.D.D.) as an illustration of a
neuropsychological syndrome commonly seen in school and patient populations
that was earlier referred to as minimal brain dysfunction (Bellak, 1979, 1985).

Since research on the cognitive structuring of narrative organization in
thematic tests does not yet have as extensive a history as Form level and other
structure scoring on the Rorschach, this chapter should be viewed as simply a
beginning sketch for future research in this exciting new area of possible neuro-
psychological dimensions on the T.A.T.

i : The Children’s Apperception Test (C.A.T.)f is a projective method or, as we

the dynamic meaningfulness of individual differences in the perception of stan-
nd dard stimuli.
nce The test is a direct descendant of the T.A.T., although it does not compete

ical iy fantasies about seeing the parents in bed together. Related to this, we wish to elicit
1al- the child’s fantasies about aggression, intra- and extra-, about acceptance by the

1Q | masturbation, toilet behavior, and the parents’ handling of and response to it. We

This test, similar to the T.A.T., is primarily concerned with the content of fund
productions. An analysis of apperceptive behavior is usually concerned with what dyna
one sees and thinks in distinction to an examination of expressive behavior, which Instr
is concerned with how one sees and thinks. We have previously discussed this andj
relationship of adaptive, expressive, and apperceptive aspects of psychological to ac
productions in the previous section on the T.A.T., in which I pointed out that the pref
Rorschach is primarily a study of the formal organization of expressive factors. As set 0
such, it is better qualified to facilitate diagnosis, if this term is taken to mean .
identifying a given person with a nosological entity as set forth in an official the |
manual on diagnosis. On the other hand, the C.A.T., like the T.A.T., is better 3 pres
able to reveal the dynamics of interpersonal relationships, of drive constellations, i som
and the nature of defenses against them. { ours
Thus, I believe that the C.A.T. may be clinically useful in determining what t chilc
dynamic factors might be related to a child’s behavior in a group, in school, or in 4 T.A
kindergarten, or to events at home. The C.A.T. may be profitable in the hands of q proc
the psychoanalyst, the psychiatrist, the psychologist, the social worker, and the the |
teacher, as well as the psychologically trained pediatrician. It may be used directly jects
’ in therapy as a play technique. After the original responses have been given, one : test.
may wish to go over them with the child in the form of play and make appropriate j
interpretations. [ red
Furthermore, the C.A.T. should lend itself particularly well to much- the |
needed longitudinal research studies on child development; if the C.A.T. were :

problems thus far studied only in psychoanalytic investigations or other cross- ie mol
sectional studies. The latter are, by necessity, reconstructions and inferences . vers
which need further confirmation and/or elaboration. In research studies and in 2
clinical use alike it should be helpful that the C.A.T. is relatively culture-free. ie We

0 | C. Theory of the C.A.T.
of i
at : ‘The theoretical considerations of the C.A.T. and the C.A.T. Supplement, pre-
of H sented later, do not differ basically from the theoretical problems and the frame
t= of reference previously discussed for the T.A.T. However, there is one additional
i aspect to be considered in the C.A.T. and the C.A.T.-S.—the use of animals as
s, ' stimuli. As has been noted earlier, on the basis of psychoanalytic experience with
in i children it was expected that children would identify more readily with animal
i than human figures. This assumption was predicated on the fact that emotional
sd : relationships to animals are easier for children to handle, and that animals are
usually smaller than adult humans and are “underdogs” like children. Animals
ay i play a prominent role in children’s phobias and as identification figures in chil-
of dren’s dreams; on a conscious level, they figure importantly as children’s friends.
in The primitivity of animal drives of oral and anal nature also increase animals’
a- : symbolic proximity for children. From the technical standpoint of a projective
ff test, it could also be assumed that the animals would offer some manifest disguise:
aggressive and other negative sentiments could more easily be ascribed to a lion
la than to a human father figure, and the child’s own unacceptable wishes could be
re, more easily ascribed to the less transparent identification figure, as compared to
as : human children.

cultures also tended to support the expectation of a high stimulus value for

In the administration of the C.A.T. account must be taken of the general prob- q ee

general, be considerably more difficult with the younger children as well as with 1

. pees 5 : 4 child \

fter all stories have been scored, record the total number of checks for each category in the blank pro- es oe .

garded as a “critical score” for that category. : oe Reprit
For the Identification measure, the equivalent of a critical score is secured by comparing the relative a be
number of checks for categories K and L. If the sum of checks for L is equal to or exceeds the sum for K, RS
identification is considered to be “confused” and contributes one unit to the total of critical scores. Sta.

the total number of checks for all categories. ee

bias When one approaches the interpretation of an apperceptive method such as
ind the C.A.T., it is best to keep some basic principles firmly in mind. The subject is
bade asked to apperceive—that is, to meaningly interpret—a situation. The subject's
lost interpretation of the stimulus in following our instruction to tell a story ex-
odi- ceeds the minimal “objective” stimulus value. He does so, by necessity, in his
the own way, which must be a function of continually present psychological forces
. which at that moment manifest themselves in relation to the given stimulus ma-
_ terial.
s of If one accepts a motivational continuity of the personality structure, one
by may use the following analogy for a testing procedure as well as psychotherapeu-
ted tic free association. If a river is sampled at various relatively close intervals, the
and chemical analyses of the content will be highly similar. Any pailful will be repre-
and sentative of the total content. This procedure is commonly followed in public
ant | health assays.
oe Now, if a new tributary joins (as compared to a new situational factor in
ae i psychological sampling), it may of course add factors about which the assayer has
oe | to know in order to account for changes in content. A primary genetic theory of
-H. personality, like psychoanalysis, maintains that the main contents of the stream
talt | will remain the primary matrix, which, after a certain point, can only be modified
a | by tributaries to a greater or lesser degree.
1 of | To leave the dangers of further analogies, we believe (and by now, ample
| experimental literature supports this belief) that interpretations of stimuli in our
the ' test material give us a valid sample of the subject’s psychic continuum known as
ind ! personality. Still in its formative stage, it is, of course, more changeable in
ade | childhood. We can learn about the motivational forces from the fact that any
| individual response is meaningful for that person; we can furthermore increase
| our insight by comparing one individual’s responses to those of others. To that
| extent, we are really studying individual differences and making inferences
about a given subject by this comparison.

it is not unreasonable to conclude that this child is preoccupied with thoughts of didn

speak of the theme of a story or of several stories. A theme may, of course, be
more or less complex. We find that particularly in our younger subjects of three 3. M:

Clinical notes 2
Again a moral is expressed, making a virtue of the acquisition of learning. : casi
In this boy’s first story, the mention of “Something funny about this— : lite
chickens don’t eat at table,” was not significant by itself; however, in the above E
story there is a similar kind of expression in the first sentence, and we must begin a Stor
to take note of the “stickler for actuality” quality and to look for any signs of rE
repetitiveness in subsequent stories. The lion’s not wearing a crown is certainly a
threat of continuity through these first three stories: the indecision in story 1 over I crad
whether mother or father is the “rooster”; the definite relegation of superior slee|
strength to the father in story 2, with identification with the mother; and the i mt
reference in this last story to the lack of crown on the lion—crown being a literal i} rai
expression of who’s “king.” 3 anot
The reference to hearing the train and its appearance “on the other side” 3 nois
could be merely a biographical reference to the child’s experience on some : don
suburban railroad or city subway, and is not meaningful by itself. The reference ' ne
to the broken track adds up with the-broken rope in story 2 to at least a raising of A
the question of possible symbolic fear of genital harm. The history did reveal a |
recent increase in masturbation. Neither of these references suggests a problem E:
of any clinical proportions. This may possibly be just a developmental factor ia
related to the younger sister’s being “different,” may be related to his being a
stickler for facts in these stories and correlate with the teachers’ complaint a
of putting them on the spot, and suggests an aggressive or obsessive connota- i
tion.

The first sentence is a repetition of this child’s characteristic literalness. It is very
Ys | unusual for children to remark on the anthropomorphic aspects of the pictures.
He did this in stories 1, 8, and 5, but not in stories 2 and 4. We should then take
} special cognizance of the kind of stories which evoke this characteristic and see

what conclusions we may be justified in drawing. Thus far, we might tentatively |
say that stories 3 and 5 have one feature in common with reference to their Her
calculated stimulus value: 3 is intended to arouse (among other things) phallic sibli
concern, whereas 5 is intended to elicit primal scene fears, and there is, of course, , asu
aclose relation between the two. We might therefore say tentatively that when the chil
boy is confronted with sexual considerations one of his defenses is to become com
concerned with “factual” and familiar realisms, or, on another level, we might say gen

prefaced in the same way when there is certainly nothing in the stimulus to cause j dep

anxiety-arousing situation, whether sexual, sibling rivalry, or whatever, provokes i fooc
this special response in this boy. What can be considered anxiety producing in i con
picture 1 can only be the fact that it is the first picture so that his frame of goo
reference has not yet been sufficiently secured. For other children, of course, the ;
picture more often has its emphasis on oral problems. I sup)
As to the primal scene per se, the main feature of his story is his omission of |
the usually seen second figure vaguely indicated in the large bed. Many children E
omit mention of figures altogether; some omit one parent or the other. We would E Stor
expect this boy to omit the father, since it has become quite apparent that his
relationship to his mother is stronger. 7
As to the specificity of the references to the various animal and insect noises, } was
specificity is a characteristic of this child and he is merely being consistent. 4 Le
However, the animals he does mention, bats, birds, and insects, are phallic E shat
symbols not infrequently seen clinically as phobias. Children’s fears of “noises in F kill]
the night” very often refer to the sounds of the parents having intercourse. : rath
The reference to “another room” is as yet obscure. Perhaps it is factually | keey
biographical; we do not know. In any case, when the mother does remove herself
to another room on the following night, the babies’ anxiety is apparently in- |
creased, since they stay up all night. All this tells us is that the subject does not I
benefit by closing his eyes to the bigger bed.

Case 2 a
com
The second case is that of an 8-year-old boy whose C.A.T. was analyzed blindly in case
the course of a class on projective techniques. The C.A.T. record was obtained by mot
the late Dr. Bela Mittelman, to whom I am very grateful, both for the record and diso
for permission to use the case of the little boy who was a psychoanalytic patient of tical
his. As it happens, I did not become familiar with the clinical data until four or | as F
five years after the initial interpretation of the C.A.T., which is presented here. fro
While such a blind method is not recommended, it happened to have been a part |
of a teaching program. '
The clinical facts are as follows: This 8-year-old boy was brought for psycho- | Ree
analytic treatment because he had suffered from eczema since his fifth month of |
life. He had been restless and cranky since the age of 2% years, when he sustained | 1
a severe burn of the right thigh. He had been doing poor work in school and was a | 2
disciplinary problem because of minor but continuous infractions of rules, such | 3
as talking, giggling, and fighting. He was unpopular with the children, got into oe
frequent scraps, and threw stones or hit them. |
His behavior toward his brother, 13 months his junior, became very aggres- i
sive after his mother became more affectionate towards the younger one, about a
year before. He frequently refused food, and he would not bathe himself or wash '
or clean his face, hands, or teeth unless there were constant reminders from his :
mother. : 4
The mother had given him little intimate contact, adhered strictly to a
feeding schedule, and was generally excitable. The child’s hands had been tied
for several weeks to prevent his scratching (when he was 2 and was hospitalized). i 5
The father and mother were divorced when the child was in the fifth month of
analysis. The father is described as close to the children but less assertive than the ;
mother. The parental divorce is reported to have renewed his mistrust of the 6
world and endangered anew his confidence in the analyst's ability to help him (he
had stoutly maintained that what he needed and expected was physical treat-
ment). He saw the world as full of hostile forces and suffered an increase in his 4
oedipal conflict and in his fear of retribution from his father.
It is easy to correlate the facts unearthed in the C.A.T. with the psychody-
namics consistent with the boy’s history: The feeling of hostility and hopelessness | ‘
consequent to his traumatic infancy appears clinically and in the C.A.T., and so !

============================================================
PAGE 315
============================================================
INTERPRETATION OF THE C.A.T. 287
/ does his secondary regression to dirtiness and the jungle and his anger toward
. mother and brother. No sleeping disorder was reported clinically, and I do not
; know whether this means that it did not exist or whether it was minor enough to
be lost in the multitude of complaints.
It must be remembered that projective techniques may point up prob-
; lems which are not clinically manifest but which may become so, under
stress or when therapy interferes with the defenses; I have frequently seen this
; (e.g., in relation to impotence inferred correctly from Rorschach signs in adult
male patients several months before they really become impotent in the course of
psychoanalytic treatment). Also, curiously enough, I had no inkling of the eczema
from the C.A.T. record. This coincides with observations that the T.A.T. may
| present a complete personality picture without permitting one to infer the chief
complaint. All the component parts of the psychodynamics (of eczema, in this
| case) are present (lack of oral gratification, hostility due to very disturbed early
mother-child relationship) but no specific reference to or indication of a skin
| disorder. Theoretically, this is a problem in need of further investigation: Prac-
tically, it is simple enough to see the skin disorder or elicit other chief complaints
| as part of the history taking; indication of this disorder need not be expected
| from the projective methods.

: FINAL REPORT: Diagnostic Impressions and Recommendations k a”
This report is predicated only on the four stories analyzed in detail. 6. Signi
In these stories our patient seems preoccupied particularly with the prob- z
lem of aggression and counteraggression. Most of the aggression seems to passiesciesisiasaise
be directed toward the younger brother, as for instance story 3, where the 1. Nate
prother appears as vermin which the patient tries to exterminate, or in
story 9, where rabbits (brother) are being hunted. In these two stories, !
as well as in story 8, which shows aggression toward the mother, the ag-
gression seems to be of a very explosive, superficially strongly controlled
nature. Because of an extremely severe though not integrated superego, the
hostile wishes are usually turned into violent intra-aggression, and. our EET
patient himself comes to harm. The brother is seen as a nuisance and the 8. Me
nother as a braggart and somewhat coercive. The father figure does not
emerge clearly in these stories except possibly as an accomplice and helper
un story 9. \
The patient perceives himself as rather helpless in coping with his | a A
problems and uses withdrawal and regression as defensive measures, as for |
instance in story 3, where he returns to the jungle, or in story 6, where i
he sees himself as troubled, suggesting that he suffers from insomnia be-
cause of nocturnal fears (probably concerning primal scene noises). H
The treatment situation and transference relationship are reflected \
in story 3 and in story 6, where the boy seems to see the therapist as a i 10. Ib
fellow-conspirator against the brother (exterminator of the vermin), who
is as useless as the carpenter called in to do away with the nocturnal i
disturbances. In fact, in the latter story, there is a suggestion that he
conceives of therapy as a further unloosing of anxiety, and wishes to leave. i
In summary, one may say that this is a fairly neurotic child with
severe problems in his relationship to his younger sibling and to his i a
mother, an inability to handle his repressed explosive hostility, and a bea
potentiality for sleeping disturbances.

Clinical notes i “The
In this story the mice and the worms probably represent the younger sibling. The z all.” (
story is particularly interesting since we can see elements of the transference’ if situat
relationship. This child sees his psychotherapist in the role of an exterminator i
(who should exterminate the brother as a way of helping the patient). Apparently, :
however, he is thus far dissatisfied with the psychotherapist, feeling that therapy i Story
does not offer him any better solutions than he-had already tried; for instance, E
permitting himself some extra-aggression seems to have boomeranged. His re- '
turn to the jungle implies not only regression but also withdrawal. Inasmuch as ny
this withdrawal is the result of a difficult reality situation, we are probably justified j today
in thinking of it as secondary withdrawal, more comparable to a phobic situation you h
(rather than of a primary withdrawal of object cathexis, as is seen in narcissistic and y
disorders). However, the indications are not quite clear, and skin conditions are who
frequently consistent with severely narcissistic disorders.

Clinical notes
This story again reflects the social level in the child’s home. We have had glimpses
| on other occasions—the mention of F) lorida, and the ease with which this child
\ procures paid professional help (the exterminator and the carpenter)—and now
| we get a realistic picture of the polite company manners observed in the home
and the child’s negative conception of his mother. The explosion already men-
| tioned in story 3 again indicates the strong aggressive feelings bottled up in this
i child, here clearly directed to the mother.
| On the one hand, we see a very strict superego which makes him comply

: : manifestly; on the other hand, he permits himself rather vicious retribution when

: : the house and, presumably, mother and the company (but perhaps himself too)

i | are blown up. This is a good example of lack of integration of the superego

; constituting at the same time too much and too little control.

Clinical notes .
This is a very complex story. At first the difference in sentiments between the
brothers and their dislike of each other is clearly set forth. The sentence, “I'll
make up a bad story about him—I hate him” may either refer manifestly to the ;
rabbit in the picture or to the brother, although dynamically there is probably no ; 3
difference. Under the impact of his emotions, this story is less well structured in : )
that there is a transition from the stimulus of a picture of a rabbit in bed to
hunters. Apparently the direct expression of aggression against the brother is
interfered with and instead of the real rabbit he uses decoys. The next twist of the
story brings about a switch of identification figures, where the hunters are being : FI:
punished for their aggression. This is probably where the intra-aggression again Ken

ae Case 3*
Kenneth was 8 years and 5 months old at the time of testing, with an I.Q. of 89 on
the Stanford-Binet. Entered in a parochial school before he was 5 years old, he
proved to be so severe a behavior problem that the sisters refused to keep him.
Things were no better in public school, where he proved to be an academic
problem as well, in his inability to learn to read.

Kenneth is tall for his age, thin, and undernourished. He wears glasses. The
mother appears to be a heavy, ignorant, placid woman who does not want her
placidity disturbed. She apparently rejects Kenneth, preferring the younger
child, a girl about 4 years old. The father, high-strung and unstable, expects his
son to be perfect, and believes that perfection in children is attained by-beating

them. He also openly shows his preference for the younger child.

The boy’s behavior at school is markedly aggressive; he has assaulted several
children quite severely, stole from the girls’ pocketbooks, removed articles from
the teacher’s desk, is constantly noisy and restless.

Kenneth does not come home for lunch as the other children do—his
mother finds it too much trouble to fix lunch for him.

| Kenneth loses bladder control by night or day and soils himself occasionally

| at school.

| Summary

Record of Main Theme (Diagnostic) and Other Main Data.

] 1. Mother seen as depriving children of basic needs, food (love). Patient feels

I unhappy. Mother seen as responding to crying. Subject feels especially

| deprived in relation to others (sister? mother?). Subject clearly identifies

i with deprived child in stimulus (chick minus bib).

2. Child and mother are aligned against father. Father doesn’t quite manage
| (wishful?). Contest is between father and child alone? (Mother is no help or

i hindrance.) Subject finally feels defeated (without ever acknowledging that

' father wins; mother has a completely passive role in this story, but somewhat

| allied with child). Fear of being weak.

' 3. Subject feels small and in danger. Fear of being devoured by father. Subject

I withdraws rapidly into small dark place; uses tricks for indrect aggression

i against father. Poor self-image.

overlooking some dimension.

and record an integrated summary on Page 4 under the appropriate headings. That way a final picture is obtained
almost immediately.

FINAL REPORT: Diagnostic Impressions and Recommendations r
These are stories of an exceedingly disturbed boy, as can be seen : 6:
from the first story to the last. The themes deal throughout with dep- \
rivation and bizarre, diffuse, all-around hostility and destructiveness, pisiaiaiaiaias
particularly in stories and 5. The hero as an identification figure 71
is either a rat or a ghost, and the vile object of deadly aggression by
incorporation (story 6). The father is seen as unremittingly aggressive,
the mother mostly as depriving and punishing, as for instance in stories |
land 10. The subject shows a great deal of hostility toward her when |
he specifies that she is put in the garbage pail head down in story 5 |
and has her head hurt repeatedly in story 4, as well as toward his baby Erereerereraras
sister. 8.1
The superego, though vicious in its intra-aggression, as in stories
6 and 9, is also inconsistent. There is no evidence of any successful
defenses. i
Although some degree of magical thinking is not unusual in children %
of this age level, story 6, which deals with the poisoned bones which are
able to kill merely by contact, transcends the bounds of expectancy for
this age. The malevolence and omnipotence which this child ascribes to
himself are distinctly pathological.
There are two suggestions in the stories that this child is probably |
enuretic: the matches which are introduced into story 8 and the running f 10. 1
water in story 10. H
In view of the general lack of structure of the stories, the lack of '
control and tendency to bizarreness, the oral features of devouring, being i
devoured, and going to sleep (Lewin's oral triad), it is very likely that i
this boy will develop into an adult psychotic with schizophrenic and
manic-depressive features. :

Postscript to Case 3

}

° Kenneth was never known to me personally. The C.A.T. record and other
H information printed in toto above was kindly made available by Miss Freyd, when

she took a course in the C.A.T. with me.

3» | As an afterthought, having brought the rest of this book up to date, it
j occurred to me to try to check on the dire prognosis, so I got in touch with Miss
| Freyd, whom I had not seen in many years. It is due to her strenuous efforts to
| trace this boy’s subsequent career that the following tragic history can be made
' available.

Kenneth moved from his hometown. After a few years, a social worker from

e the new domicile requested information on him because at about age 13 he

if | assaulted his sister sexually, threatened to kill her if she told anyone, and when
| discovered in the act by his mother at one time almost strangled the mother. The
| father, who previously had told the school’s social worker to mind her own
business, that he knew how to handle the boy, then told the social worker she
| should take care of him—“he is all yours.”

to Ken was then sent to a state school. He ran away several times. At some later

to time, according to a relative, he seemed to adjust better for several years, worked,

Aa got married, and had a daughter. After about three years of marriage, he met
i another young woman who became pregnant by him. Meeting her in a park near

============================================================
PAGE 340
============================================================
i
312 CHAPTER 14 i
his childhood home, he strangled her to death. He was executed at age 28, just : Pi
about 20 years after taking the test reported here. i He
The C.A.T. report that he was an exceedingly disturbed boy was hardly : Fa
overstated. Extreme aggression and hostility are noted throughout. The report j 4
failed to predict overt mayhem, though that fact was obvious from the behavioral i
report. What the C.A.T. supplies is the bizarreness of the aggression and the } S
general severe pathology. It has been impossible to obtain institutional records to | bear :
ascertain whether a psychosis was diagnosed at any point. The crime Ken was Story ;
executed for certainly sounds like a direct repetition of his earlier tendencies to : wants
choke someone to death, and most likely was the result of sudden loss of control regres
rather than premeditation. This makes the sentence a puzzling one. It is unlikely manif
that any amount of therapy at that late date would really have made him a safe the he
person to have around, but at the same time it is very unlikely that he could have anoth
been a person of sound mind who was aware of the consequences of his act while ee
engaged in it. It is probably a reflection on the nature of our criminal justice that father
this man was executed rather than hospitalized. being
This whole story underlines points I have made elsewhere (Bellak & Barton, assum
1969): that it is not only necessary to screen children psychologically at school “the t
entrance, but also to have the legal right to insist upon treatment, removal from a —
pathological home, and/or treatment of the parents, if necessary without their : rival.
voluntary consent. Like the mother of Lee Harvey Oswald, this boy’s father ie
rejected professional help until it was clearly too late. Society can ill afford the siblin
burden of criminal psychosis, nor is it fair to innocent children to insist upon their | rival
parents’ right to mistreat and cripple them. signif

he Story 2 is certainly a very meager one. All that attracts attention is, “the big
to bear who got so big”—which by itself surely barely deserves any speculation.
as Story 3, however, demonstrates repeatedly that the subject rejects the clothing,
to wants to “sit in a dirty chair with no clothes on.” This would indicate a wish to
ol regress to an earlier stage. Still, we have no idea why. Then, in picture 9, the most
ly manifest clue is contained in the fact that the bunny “may put another bunny up
fe the house.” This definitely sounds as though the subject is preoccupied with
e another baby coming into the house. Those psychoanalytically trained will be able
le to see a symbolic restatement of this thought in the running upstairs and the
ut father bear coming out from the basement coupled with an apparent memory of
being told to go to bed perhaps in connection with some sexual activity. Our
1, assumption now may find some corroboration in the brief reference in story 2,
| “the big bear who got so big,” which may refer to the mother’s pregnancy. Then
a we can understand his regressive pattern in story 3 in relation to the arrival of the
re rival. These were the conclusions-we arrived at on blind analysis of these stories.
r A check with data from the social worker showed that it was not actually a
J sibling, but a little cousin that had arrived in the home. Since the aunt and the
r rival (her son) lived in the same household with the subject, the psychological
significance was the same. The kindergarten teacher was replete with con-
firmation of the subject’s behavioral problems. We had occasion to consider
further the subject’s statement that the hero “wants to have a lot of hair around
him.” The inference one could make is that he has compared himself to the father
and wants to have hair on the chest and in the pubic area also. Outstanding
among the behavioral problems as reported by the teacher was the fact that the
subject explored his little girl playmates with a great deal of interest.

This record can serve as an example of relatively poor returns in a small
child wherein each story by itself is quite disappointing unless and until one can
bring each story in meaningful relation to the others. Nevertheless, the usefulness
of the C.A.T., in this case, becomes quite clear. The teacher and social worker
knew that he was a behavioral problem with excessive sexual interest in little girls.
Our test relates his behavioral difficulties to rivalry with a sibling-like figure, and a
preoccupation with procreation. Having established these relationships, it should
be relatively simple to discuss this with the child apropos of his stories: that he
must be angry about the new arrival; must wonder where babies come from; and
so on. At the same time, the social worker might attempt to decrease his sexual

| stimulation by whatever means the circumstances might permit, and instruct the
| mother about handling him.

Brief Analysis
In both card | stories, the children eat badly, are naughty, and antagonize the big
chicken, who punishes them and sends them away. In the second testing, an
aggressive animal is introduced, a fox, who eats up the mother and is, in turn,
drowned for his misdeeds, whereupon the child reverts to an obsessive preoc-
cupation with the weather which went on all through the testing. In the story to
card 3, in the first session, he is anxiously concerned with the idea that one has to
be careful or else one is devoured. In the second session, he wants to do away with
the card altogether by scaling it out the window. There is much more evidence of
violence and anal regression here with the lion “pooing” on his chair. The
aggressive orality now relates specifically to the castrating notion of biting off the
tail. There is also the suggestive evidence of explosive emotional tension in
connection with the dynamite and the wish for a hurricane. In story 5, in the first
j testing, the reference to smoke and fire suggest a great deal of aggressive urethral
| sexual preoccupation, as does the reference to crying. This would be most sug-
| gestive of a history of enuresis (which we were unable to check on) but is certainly
| consistent with his aggressive behavior, including the aggressive need to show off.
| The second testing gives a much less clear-cut story, except that the little bears
i run out when the parents come home and are never discovered. This is followed
\ by some reference to figures and the discussion again of violent weather, in this
| case a fast wind. Story 6 in the first session introduces water, supporting the
| notion expressed in story 5, and again a preoccupation with oral incorporation.
| Story 6 in the second session has to do with being walled up with mud and

watchful nighttime observations. This is suggestive of insomnia, perhaps associ-
ated with oral incorporation fantasies, and then again comes the preoccupation
with numbers, windspeeds, and the weather—his restlessness is also indicated by A S
the reference to running.
An examination of test material suggests not only the marked pathology
consistent with the clinical report of aggression and showing off but also that the TO
process is worsening. Judging by the leaving of the stimulus, the inappropriate
material, and very poor drive control, this boy is probably on the way towards a
psychotic condition. Obsessive preoccupation and acting out have so far served as
brakes on the ego disintegration. A school psychiatrist who saw the child sus-
pected that he might be schizophrenic.

A. Purpose of the C.A.T.-S,
The C.A.T. Supplement (C.A.T.-S.) was designed to supply pictures which might
illuminate situations not necessarily pertaining to universal problems, but which occur
often enough to make it desirable to learn more about them as they exist in a good
many children.

Ten pictures have been designed (Figure 15-1), any single one of which

‘ may be presented to children in addition to the regular C.A.T. For instance, «
C.A.T.-S. picture 5 may be given to children with a temporary or permanent
physical disability or with a history of disability. It might permit one to learn about

| the psychological effects of this somatic problem upon the specific child. Or
children with any kind of psychosomatic disorder or hypochondriasis might
project these onto the stimulus. Picture 10 may permit us to learn what fantasies a
boy or girl may have about the mother’s pregnancy. If, for example, a child is
brought to a clinic with a number of behavioral problems, and the history shows
that the mother is currently pregnant or has delivered relatively recently, then
this picture may permit one to learn about the possible relationship between the
behavior problems and the fantasies concerning the family event.

In short, the C.A.T.-S. may be used in specific situations for the purpose of
eliciting specific themes—as seem indicated (and as discussed below).

A further use of the C.A.T.-S. may lie in its usefulness as material for play
techniques. Even though establishing proper rapport will obtain longer and
better stories from children than the beginner is likely to think, there remain

\ children severely enough disturbed to be unable to relate stories. For such sub-
| jects it may be expedient to make all the pictures of the C.A.T.-S. available at once,
i upon a table (arranged from 1 to 10, in three rows, the last row having four
| pictures), and to let them see them, handle them, arrange, and talk about them as
| they will. All of the child’s remarks and behavior should be carefully recorded.
i Also, such use of the pictures may encourage storytelling in children less able to
| comply immediately with instructions. It should be mentioned, however, that this

| at Vassar College, and C. Fear for supplying data for the CAT-S.

: A SUPPLEMENT TO THE C.A.T. 325

' Proper rapport between child and administrator is most important. It is best

b to get to know the child before administration, to play games first so as to let him

k become accustomed to the examiner and to the situation and to reduce anxiety to

L a minimum.

| ; To younger children particularly, the C.A.T. or the C.A.T.-S. may best be

H presented as a storytelling game. By far the most successful technique has been to

q make the test administration part of a group situation as often as possible. In a

] nursery, for example, one may choose the most fear-free and friendly child first,

E allowing it to appear that this is something of a distinction and something pleasant

' and interesting. If the first is thus successfully carried off, the rest of the children
will compete about who may be next and will be cooperative and interested.

E Children usually do not mind at all when recordings are made either by
hand or by instrument. It is simple to flatter their narcissism by telling them that
one’will be able thus to read or play the stories back to them (should they inquire

| about the recording.)

| Again, it is important not to permit a child to see more than one picture at a
time (unless the play technique is being used) and to conceal (in a desk drawer, for
instance) the others lest the child be impatient to cut short the current story in his
eagerness to see the next picture.

When the C.A.T.-S. is used as an instrument of play technique, all pictures
of the Supplement—and possibly also those of the regular C.A.T.—are exposed
simultaneously and, as previously stated, all remarks, manipulations, picture :
constellations, and combinations are recorded.

C. Inquiry
Special attention needs to be directed to the importance of knowing the behav-
ioral conditions and the real-life situation of the subject. It is entirely true that
; “blind” interpretations of stories (i.e., interpretations of stories without knowl-
edge of any other data) may lead to impressive and startlingly accurate insights.
Nevertheless, for clinical use it is important that the projective data be seen in conjunction
he with as much information about the reality situation as possible.

The inquiry should be directed toward that part of the reality most closely
he linked with the stories. One should ascertain as often as possible where specific
Wwe names, places, and other precise references in a story come from. Ifa plotis taken
ns from TV, radio, films, fairytales, comic strips, or other sources, it is important for
“es the examiner to know it. This does not mean that the story is useless—on the

contrary—there will doubtless be individual distortions of the original source
S, | which will be particularly illuminating. Even if the story should be a faithful
d. reproduction of the original source (TV, etc.,) it will nevertheless be subjectively
indicative that this specific story was elicited by the stimulus card.

Of particular importance for the inquiry is that attempts be made to dis-
cover whether a given story or certain details of one reflect a factual or a wishful
state of affairs. For instance, if a father figure is seen as especially patient,

he | : nurturant, and protective, it should be a simple matter to establish whether this
ed reflects the child’s actual conception of the father or whether the father is the
| opposite in reality and the stories thus primarily reflect a wish.

Thus, such data, when based upon large enough numbers, may permit us to
deal with a record in terms of how it meets certain norms and will help us identify

a deviation (also such a normative scheme may be useful to demonstrate develop-
mental trends).

For instance, if more than half of our sample introduce the mother in
picture 8, it would not be reasonable to infer from such an introduction in any
individual record that there is a clinically significantly greater dependence upon
the mother than in most children of this age. On the other hand, if 38 out of 40
children speak of picture 2 as a schoolroom situation, any child who does not do
so merits special attention. Sure enough, the records of our two deviants are very

informative. One of them says this:

i A number of sociocultural studies include both normative comparisons of

— Lindzey (1952) proposed that thematic content which can be directly connected
to elements in the presented stimulus is less likely to be significant in interpreta-
tion than that which has been added or is only indirectly related to the stimulus.
This statement implies that thematic material not closely tied to the stimulus is
more likely to be relevant to overt behavior.

Poni Kagan (1956) investigated the problem of manifest versus latent levels of
fantasy, and presented groups of aggressive and nonaggressive boys with pictures
ambiguous for aggression and pictures which implied aggressive actions. Ambig-

i uous pictures did not differentiate between groups, whereas aggressive children
ntial responded to aggressive stimuli with significantly more aggressive stories. It
gest would seem that aggressive boys had less anxiety about telling aggressive stories to
and aggressive stimuli.

= ¥ The Senior Apperception Technique (S.A.T.)* is an extension of the T.A.T.
ngful designed to elucidate the problems of elderly individuals. When the S.A.T. was
pur- : designed in 1973, 10 percent of the population, or over 20 million Americans,
nee were over 65 years old. In intervening years, that number has increased to 30
sory. million in 1988, or 12 Percent} and is increasing steadily. In 1990, Donnelley
ed to Marketing Information Services** estimated the U.S. population over 65 to
already be above 33 million; a 1 percent increase in only two years. Our society has
Mee been no better prepared for the population explosion of the aged than it has been
oa for the ecological effects of population growth, the development of atomic power,
ne or for any of the other changes in geometric Proportions so typical of our era. /
The problems of the aged are therefore plentiful, as described, for instance,
by Sloate (1974) in comprehensive reviews published by the American Psychiatric
Association (1973), ina volume with sociological as well as Psychological implica-
tions by Geist (1968), and in a practical handbook about aging by Bellak (1975).
It is difficult to describe the aged, even as defined for people above 65 years
old. And even if subdivided, as has been suggested, into young, old, and old-old,
the most frequently complicating factor concerning a general statement of the
aged is the economic factor. By and large it seems to hold true that the relatively
better off someone is economically, the relatively more benign is their aging. The
blue-collar person, often having lived a harder life, is less able to be concerned
with an often more expensive diet, is generally living under less favorable circum-
stances, and is likely to be significantly worse off than a well-to-do person. Also,
the blue collar, lower-middle class, and lower-class aged population has devel-
oped fewer resources, having usually come home from a day of labor and not
finding more energy than for television watching. Such a person will usually have .
done little networking and perhaps will not have developed a taste for concerts
{ and theatre. The individual is unlikely to play chess or find an enjoyment in
literature. The net result is a person with few resources, a higher incidence of
illness, and generally finding aging a much more vexing problem. In distinction, a
| middle-class person of age 70 might still play tennis, go skiing, or travel. That
i does not keep this person free of physical complaints, problems of loneliness, and
i fear of debilitating illness and death, but it does ameliorate and alleviate some of
| the problems of aging. In constructing the Senior Aptitude Test ($.A.T.) with the

foreground. It is the only consistent way in which rivalry for a son’s favors
emerges.

The teenager is often patronizingly referred to as “a teenager on the

“spread out.” Indirect allusion to the sexuality implied in the drawing emerges.

E. Data Concerning the Senior Apperception Technique of them

By tradition, the S.A.T. falls into the class of projective techniques: a stimulus is Hae
presented to a subject whose responses in the form of stories, words and behavior Ne
are scrutinized for whatever they may reveal about that subject. made fc
In 1950 Bellak introduced the study of the defenses in projective techniques frequer
(1950) and enlarged on the application of ego psychology to them in a paper in feelings
1954 (1954) and further extended the concept in his volume on the T.A.T. and ou
C.A.T. (1971). hundre
Cognitive style is the term now generally used to comprise the totality of discuss
responses, somewhat anticipated in the above references. To the extent that we female:
study each person as an individual, idiosyncratic ideographic ways of dealing with socioec
a particular stimulus situation affect the process we are studying. For this reason, from al
Herman Rorschach’s term for his inkblot inquiry was a “Versuch,” an experi- the S.A
ment, and itis still by far the best term and much to be preferred to “test,” with its A
normative connotations in American psychology. For this reason, the title Senior of wor
Apperception Technique is preferable to Senior Apperception Test. length
This is true for the T.A.T. and C.A.T. also. In responses to these picture A
stimuli, we are dealing with the unique Gestalt of thought processes, of structure concre
as well as content. 65 yea

The thesis by Nancy Altobello (1973) studies hope and despair by utilizing the
1 and S.A.T. It produced interesting results contradicting Neugarten’s (1972) hypothe-
elicit ses of disengagement that elderly persons, if given a relatively supporting social
ole in environment, will choose personal involvement.
The “disengagement theory,” originally stated by Cummings and Henry
tures (1961), was investigated and later propounded by Neugarten. She originally
‘null proposed that elderly persons experience a decrease in emotional involvement
ories during the aging process and therefore withdraw from those activities which once
ighly | * We would like to express our appreciation to Dr. Bernard Landis, Associate Professor at the State
