Overall the control group of students did not differ substantially from the
elderly. The only notable differences were between the two sexes.
In an investigation of the elderly person’s psychosexual concerns and the
effects that aging may have upon their sexual ideation, Lynette Ackerly used the
: S.A.T., as well as the T.A.T. and Rorschach (Ackerly, 1973).
; Ackerly’s hypotheses were that older people will reveal their interest in sex
7 through stories they will tell to various picture stimuli; that the T.A.T. would elicit
2 a higher rate of sexual imagery than the S.A.T. because of stereotyped attitudes
2 about sexual feelings in older people; that there would be a higher percentage of
5 sexual images in the elderly as compensation for unfulfilled sexual longings; and
e that individual differences, more than age differences, should be reflected in the
a degrees of sexual responsiveness to the projective materials.
e Her fifteen subjects ranged from 65 to 86 years, with an average of 75.6
eS years. Of the seven men, two were single, three widowed, and two presently
g married. Among the eight women, one was single, four widowed, and three
: presently married. She studied the frequency of seven themes: depression and
: loneliness; competition, antagonism, and aggression; discouragement and disap-
2, pointment; security and health concerns; needs for nurturance; affiliation and
ly compassion; and sexuality.
e Subjects were given 21 S.A.T. cards, 4 T.A.T. cards, and the 10 Rorschach
e cards. Seven of the subjects were given the S.A.T. first while eight were given the
T.A.T. and Rorschach first.
i- The most striking finding was that sexuality did not drop out as people age;
re among the seven themes, it was fifth in prevalence on the S.A.T., but second
highest on the T.A.T. Generally, the older half of the subjects showed as much
1e interest in sexual subjects as the younger half. No significant difference was
of found between the level of sexual interest in men and women. There were
yw marked individual differences.
rd Deanna Toone investigated whether old age is accompanied by a constricted
its world view. She considered the degree and breadth of responses to S.A.T.
pictures as‘an indication of respondent's engagement in the external world and
be hypothesized that older subjects would score lower on all measures than the
nt younger group.
nd In her review of the literature, she calls attention to the importance of

Garland administered a questionnare and ten S.A.T. plates to two groups of criteria

There were no significant differences between the two age groups as far as
. the kinds of dependency themes mentioned. In keeping with a view that re-

not related to dependency; it was unclear from this sample whether or not marital
status might be related to dependency. Garland also divided her older subjects
into two age groups: those over 70 and those younger. The older women aver-
aged less themes of dependency than the younger ones.

to count the number of words relating to hope, despair, affiliative tendencies, and Y

Figure 18-1 shows this report blank which is a logical extension of the forms ‘
developed for T.A.T. and the C.A.T. It permits recording not only of these tests
but also of the basic data of an entire test battery. The emphasis is again on the
practicality of an overview and the provision of a systematic framework for the
formulation of diagnostic inferences.
The Report Blank is meant primarily to be used by the psychologist for
imparting information he has derived from a detailed study of the tests to the Test Behavior
referring psychiatrist, psychologist, or social worker; some psychologists might
also want to use it as their worksheet, supplemented by scratch paper and neces- i
sary modifications, though it is not specifically designed for this purpose.
However, the Report Blank should lend itself especially well to teaching and
training purposes.
It was designed in the hope that it will:
1. Make test reporting intellectually less of a chore by providing a frame of sae
reference and a set of variables which in part need only to be check rated—
rather than having to write a lengthy essay. ae
2. Provide a somewhat standardized basis for test reporting. The problems of
test reporting are numerous (Bellak, 1959). One of the most frequent Theray
problems is doubtless that the peruser of the report does not get enough of
an idea of the test reporter’s progression from raw data to inference.
3. Provide a more orderly form in which to submit the report than the fre-
quently used personal stationery or blank pieces of paper. It will make careiae
individual test reports comparable to others.
For the purpose of providing an overall view of the data, the foldout style,
which has been found helpful in the Bellak Short Form T.A.T. and C.A.T. Blank,
of the actual form is arranged so that the summary and the final report can be in
simultaneous view, both for test reporter and test user.

An indirect therapeutic intervention using T.A.T cards in the treatment of a 13-year-old boy,
nic who had accidentally killed a younger relative seven years ago, is described. Using a dialectical
approach, the cotherapists presented contrasting T.A.T. stories in an, attempt to reflect the boy's
inner conflicts, ambivalencies, and distorted perceptions. This approach provided the boy with :
id alternate and more positive ways of perceiving and dealing with reality and enabled him to
ity relate to and cope with the taboo topic of the traumatic incident in a relatively short time. It is
suggested that the use of this approach in highly sensitive situations, where considerable caution
est is warranted, should be explored with various age groups.

33
bis Reviews the examination protocol recommended when administering the T.A.T. to mentally
it retarded (MR) clients and examines studies on the use of the procedure with MR persons. It is
recommended that directions be concrete and explicit, and the tester may want the client to
explain his or her understanding to ensure adequate comprehension. Examples may be given
IY, and the subject can be prompted, but questions should not be suggestive. Testing the limits of the
response is suggested when clarification is necessary. Stories should be interpreted in the context
B. of the individual's intellectual functioning and cognitive complexity. Studies illustrate the
n. usefulness of the procedure for understanding MR clients from broken homes, their motivation
of for achievement, the fear of runaways, and the psychodynamics of subjects diagnosed as having
psychopathic personalities. Three additional studies illustrate the examination of aggressive
ae fantasies of MR criminals. It is concluded that the T.A.T. is an excellent personality assessment
ist instrument for MR individuals.

é Students in Introductory Psychology (N = 75) were administered the Narcissism-Projective

An adapted version of the McClellands’s Thematic Apperception Test, a measure of the power

é suggesting that Winter’s Revised Measure is a compound measure.
